title: Short Stuff: Blueprints
summary: Short Stuff episode on blueprints and the color Prussian blue, the conclusion of a two-part series on colors. The hosts explain cyanotype, the photographic process discovered by John Herschel in 1842 that produced white lines on Prussian blue paper, and how Anna Atkins used it for her 1843 book of British algae photographs. They describe the origin of Prussian blue in Berlin, accidentally created by dyemaker Diesbach and alchemist Dippel, its naming after the Prussian army uniforms and its mixed reception after Waterloo. The episode then covers the decline of blueprints: the diazo (diazo white print) process, which gave black or gray lines on white, its fading in sunlight and ammonia regulations, Xerography and the dry copier process, and the return of pen plotters.

segments.title: Opening and series context
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the episode as the conclusion of a two-part series on colors, and preview Prussian blue and the blueprint.

segments.title: Cyanotype process and John Herschel
segments.summary: John Herschel discovered in 1842 that Prussian blue is light-reactive, enabling copies via cyanotype. Anna Atkins's 1843 book Photographs of British Algae was the first published photography book, made with cyanotype. Architects adopted the process to copy drawings; the hosts explain the white-lines-on-blue reversal and the dark-room aspect.

segments.title: Origin of Prussian blue in Berlin
segments.summary: Prussian blue was accidentally created in a Berlin lab shared by alchemist Johann Conrad Dippel and dyemaker Diesbach, when Diesbach borrowed potash and ox blood was involved. It was first called Berlin blue and later Prussian blue after the Prussian army uniforms; its reception varied by nationality, with the Prussians' role at Waterloo.

segments.title: Decline of blueprints and the diazo process
segments.summary: Blueprints fell out of use as labor-intensive cyanotype gave way to the diazo white print, which gave black or gray lines on white, and later xerographic copiers. The hosts note the dry xerographic process and the Xerox name.

segments.title: Diazo fading, ammonia, and digital printing
segments.summary: Diazo prints faded in sunlight and were not archival; ammonia use and regulations led to its decline in the 1970s through early 2000s, and cheaper digital printers replaced it.

segments.title: Pen plotters and modern plotting
segments.summary: Pen plotters, which drew multiple copies at once, have returned as computerized machines; a sign-maker friend used plotters to cut designs from computer files.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts wrap up the short stuff episode, with the standard closing credits and iHeartRadio attribution.
